We work to strengthen the capacities of national stakeholders in economic management, strategic planning, and the implementation of reforms. At the same time, we promote applied research and innovation to foster inclusive and sustainable growth that addresses local economic challenges.

news1.title: Inaugural Lecture on the Occasion of CAPEC's 30th Anniversary
news1.excerpt: CAPEC celebrated its 30th anniversary on October 8 and 9, 2024, in Abidjan, in the presence of Mr. Emmanuel Ahoutou KOFFI, Minister and Director of Cabinet of the Vice-President, who delivered a remarkable inaugural lecture. He praised CAPEC's impact on public policy in Côte d'Ivoire and within the UEMOA-ECOWAS region, while encouraging the institution to innovate in response to climate, technological, and industrial challenges. This anniversary provided an opportunity to review three decades of expertise and outline prospects for inclusive and sustainable development.
news1.mot:
CAPEC contributes to tackling the high cost of living
  1. At the invitation of the General Secretariat of the Presidency of Côte d’Ivoire, CAPEC has been actively contributing to efforts to address the high cost of living since July 2021, through the study “Recent evolution of the cost of living in Côte d’Ivoire”. The objective was to assess the magnitude of the phenomenon as experienced and perceived by the population, identify widely consumed goods, products and services whose prices increased, analyze price formation mechanisms as well as the structure of prices for the items identified. The recommendations helped strengthen ongoing measures to reduce the cost of living in Côte d’Ivoire. At UNDP’s request, CAPEC also carried out (December 2022 to June 2023) an “impact study of the Russia–Ukraine crisis on the Ivorian economy”. The results and recommendations served as a basis for various policy notes and helped enrich programs and projects of UN agencies in Côte d’Ivoire.

CAPEC, expert in foresight analysis
  1. In March 2020, CAPEC was selected by the West Africa Subregional Office of the Economic Commission for Africa to support ECOWAS in drafting its ECOWAS 2050 Foresight Vision. CAPEC received congratulations from the Council of Ministers of Planning and Integration of the ECOWAS area during its session of November 9, 2021. The Vision 2050 document was adopted by ECOWAS Heads of State in Accra in December 2021. Based on the reference scenario “Africa’s torch”, the following statement is the foundation of the Vision 2050: “A fully integrated Community of peoples in a peaceful and prosperous region with strong institutions that respects fundamental freedoms and works for inclusive and sustainable development.”
  2. For UNDP Madagascar, CAPEC conducted in 2021 the study “Madagascar’s Foresight Vision 2030–2040–2063”. Based on an in-depth diagnostic study of the country’s characteristics, an examination of population aspirations and key actors, a structural analysis of the Malagasy system and the identification of possible and desirable futures for prosperity, Madagascar’s foresight vision was formulated as follows: “Madagascar, a regional economic hub endowed with strong and stable institutions, founded on a society with high human capital, optimal management of natural resources and climate resilience, for the harmonious and sustainable flourishing of peoples.”
  3. The WAEMU Commission selected the CAPEC–CUAPTD consortium (UNESCO Chair in Anticipation, Foresight and Sustainable Territories) to develop WAEMU’s Vision 2040. The vision project adopted by the Commissioners is stated as follows: “WAEMU, a sustainably peaceful and prosperous area, endowed with strong institutions, a catalyst for integration in West Africa, open to Africa, with a consolidated strategic position in the world.”

motDuDirecteur.title: Director's Message
motDuDirecteur.paragraph1: It is with great pleasure that I welcome you to the official website of the Policy Analysis Unit for Economic Policies at CIRES (CAPEC). This digital space is intended to be a dynamic showcase of our institution — a place for sharing information and dialogue in support of applied economic research and public policy decision-making.
motDuDirecteur.paragraph2: Since its creation in 1993, CAPEC has positioned itself as a major player in policy analysis in Côte d'Ivoire and Africa. Our mission is to produce rigorous analyses based on reliable, evidence-based data to inform the strategic choices of public decision-makers, private-sector actors, civil society, development partners and all stakeholders involved in economic and social development. It serves as a bridge between academia and development actors.
motDuDirecteur.paragraph3: Our renewed website has been designed to meet your needs and is now the preferred channel to keep you updated daily on our achievements. Through this site, we invite you to explore our research work, publications, ongoing projects, analytical tools, as well as our training and knowledge dissemination activities. Please visit our website regularly to access up-to-date information about our activities.
motDuDirecteur.paragraph4: We firmly believe that shared knowledge is a powerful lever for transformation. For this reason, CAPEC is committed to remaining accessible, open and attentive to society’s needs.
motDuDirecteur.closing: Happy browsing to all, and thank you for your interest in our work.

1.title: Director of CAPEC
1.bio:
Alban A. E. Ahouré is a Full Professor of Economics at Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny in Abidjan (since 2021) and Director of the Policy Analysis Unit for Economic Policies at CIRES (CAPEC) since 2011. He earned his PhD in Economics from Kobe University (Japan, 2006) and specializes in applied microeconomics, labor economics and human resources, institutional economics, game theory and policy evaluation.

He has coordinated numerous studies on competitiveness, taxation, the private sector, informality, agriculture, governance and development prospects for national, regional (WAEMU, ECOWAS) and international institutions (AfDB, World Bank, UNDP, WFP, FAO, UNICEF, etc.).

Author of several books and peer-reviewed articles, his research focuses on employability, economic inclusion, inclusive business models and structural transformation in Africa.

Elected in 2024 as an Honorary Member of the Royal European Academy of Doctors (RAED) and featured repeatedly in the Who's Who in Côte d'Ivoire, he actively contributes to scientific debate and development policy in Africa.

3.title: Researcher - Head of Administrative Management
3.bio: KRAMO Kouakou Germain holds a PhD in Economics. He is a researcher at the Policy Analysis Unit for Economic Policies at CIRES (CAPEC) where he has coordinated or contributed to several projects and studies on the Ivorian economy and other African countries. With around ten years of research experience, Dr KRAMO is Head of Administrative Management at CAPEC and an Assistant Professor at the Faculty of Economics and Management at Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny. His research interests include public finance, international trade, economic integration, intellectual property rights and productivity.

4.title: Researcher at the Economic Policy Analysis Unit (CAPEC)
4.bio: BECHO Isabelle (née N'DRI) is an economist holding a PhD in Economics from Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny (Cocody) and a microprogram diploma in Applied Development Economics from Université Laval. She is a teacher-researcher at the Virtual University of Côte d'Ivoire (UVCI) and a researcher at CAPEC. Her expertise includes impact evaluation of public policies, poverty analysis, vulnerability assessment, political economy and governance, gender analysis, firm analysis, informal sector analysis, inclusive finance, microfinance, development economics, quantitative and qualitative methodologies and data analysis. She has worked on gender, vulnerability and violent extremism projects, collaborated with UN Women, and led research with USAID on COVID-19 policy impacts on women and youth in West Africa. She has also consulted for Equal Access on projects to reduce violent extremism through economic and social inclusion of youth. She teaches microeconomics, data analysis and research methods to students and public/private professionals and is member of scientific associations such as the International Association of Francophone Microfinance Researchers (AICFM) and the Association of Women Researchers of Côte d'Ivoire (AFEMCI).

5.title: Environmental Economist & Senior Researcher at CAPEC
5.bio: Mr. BEKE Tite Ehuitché is an Associate Professor at the Faculty of Economics and Management, Université FHB (Abidjan). He holds a PhD in Environmental Economics and is a Senior Researcher at CAPEC. His publications and study reports focus on resilient agricultural value chains in the face of climate change, food security, the green economy, just ecological transition and green jobs. He is a member of the operational GJAM (Green Jobs Assessment Model) team and Team21 Côte d’Ivoire.

6.title: Economist Researcher at CAPEC
6.bio: Dr TRAORE Nohoua holds a PhD in Development Economics from Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny and a professional postgraduate diploma in Project Management. He is currently an Assistant Professor at Université Alassane Ouattara and an economist researcher at the CAPEC. Dr Traoré has contributed to several international research projects funded by IDRC focusing on firm performance in francophone Sub-Saharan Africa, economic inclusion of youth and women, inclusive entrepreneurship and COVID-19 impacts. His national contributions include work on informal sector supervision, tobacco product taxation, entrepreneur status, tax optimization and exemptions, privatization, and private sector competitiveness. He has also trained fiscal administration staff across francophone Africa on research methods applied to taxation for the African Tax Administration Forum (ATAF). He publishes in international journals and is a member of scientific committees including the African Tax Research Network and Sustainability, Research & Innovation Network.

7.title: Researcher and Development Economist at CAPEC
7.bio: Holder of a PhD in Economics from ENSEA (Abidjan), with strong training in statistics and mathematics, he is a development economist and researcher at CAPEC, responsible for data management. His combined expertise enables rigorous applied economic research. His work focuses on financial stability, public debt, structural transformation and policy evaluation using advanced econometric methods to provide robust, decision-oriented analyses.

8.title: Researcher at the Economic Policy Analysis Unit (CAPEC)
8.bio: Dr KOUADIO holds a PhD in Economics from Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny (Cocody). As a teacher-researcher and consultant, he has conducted numerous studies for international and local institutions. At CAPEC he contributed to many research projects, progressing from research assistant to associate researcher. He is a member of AfricaLics and his research interests include development economics, innovation management, firm economics, knowledge economy, digital economy, transport economics and quantitative techniques (statistics and econometrics).

9.title: Macroeconomist Researcher at CAPEC
9.bio: Kacou Yves Thierry Kacou holds a PhD in Economics from the University of Ulsan (South Korea). He is a lecturer-researcher at INPHB (Yamoussoukro) and a macroeconomist researcher at CAPEC. He has contributed to studies on fiscal policy, economic modelling and forward-looking analysis, including development of a multi-sector DSGE model for the Ivorian economy and analysis of macroeconomic consequences of infrastructure delays and climate risk adaptation in WAEMU countries. His interests include public policy impact, applied econometrics and macroeconomic modelling.

11.title: Macroeconomist Researcher at CAPEC
11.bio: Touré Talnan Aboulaye has been a lecturer-researcher in economics at INP-HB (Yamoussoukro) since September 2023 and a junior macroeconomist researcher at CAPEC. He has contributed to studies on the competitiveness challenges of the Ivorian economy, the impact of electricity price increases (policy brief), the national strategy for resource mobilization (SNRMT), socio-economic impact assessment of tax exemptions, and the evaluation of fiscal measures such as changes in corporate tax regimes (BIC). He holds a PhD in Economics from Kobe University (Japan) and his research interests include monetary, banking and financial economics and fiscal policy.

news17.title: Japan Corner - JICA - CAPEC International Conference
news17.excerpt: Félix Houphouët-Boigny University of Cocody hosted the Japan Corner - JICA - CAPEC International Conference on the theme: 'Advancing industrialization and improving labor productivity: a path for the development of the Ivorian economy'.
news17.mot:
Japan Corner - JICA - CAPEC International Conference

On February 22, 2024, Félix Houphouët-Boigny University of Cocody hosted the Japan Corner - JICA - CAPEC International Conference on the theme: ‘Advancing industrialization and improving labor productivity: a pathway for the development of the Ivorian economy’.

The opening ceremony brought together key figures, including Ms. KABA Nialé, Minister of Economy, the JICA Resident Representative, the Ambassador of Japan and Prof. MITANI Naoki, who presented Japan’s human resource development model.

He reviewed three historical phases that contributed to Japan’s economic success despite limited natural resources:

  1. 1. Education and modernization (Edo–Meiji era).
  2. 2. Building a skilled workforce (Taishō–Shōwa era).
  3. 3. Educational reforms and lifelong learning (post-war period).

These Japanese strategies—universal access to education, in-company training and fair assessment of skills—offer valuable lessons to strengthen productivity and worker motivation in Côte d’Ivoire.

Ms. KABA, Minister of Economy, highlighted the relevance of this model to support Côte d’Ivoire’s socio-economic transformation.

news19.title: Launch of the SPIA Project in Côte d'Ivoire
news19.excerpt: A new dynamic for Ivorian agriculture with the launch of the SPIA project in Côte d'Ivoire.
news19.mot:
• Launch of the SPIA project in Côte d’Ivoire: a new momentum for Ivorian agriculture

As part of its research program, the Standing Panel on Impact Assessment (SPIA), in collaboration with Félix Houphouët-Boigny University through CAPEC and the University of Bordeaux, launched in Côte d’Ivoire an ambitious pilot project aimed at developing integrated approaches to evaluating agricultural innovations. This project takes place in a context of agricultural sector transformation, marked by a strong need for effective innovations, rigorous evaluations and the valorization of scientific results.

The project’s main objective is to identify agricultural innovations linked to the CGIAR network, analyze their adoption by farmers, and study the public policies that foster their dissemination. Ultimately, the goal is to produce reliable and useful data to inform development decisions in agriculture and strengthen the contribution of research to more effective public policies.

The first phase consists of identifying existing innovations, mapping the areas concerned and analyzing their level of adoption. The project is structured around three pillars:

  • An inventory of agricultural innovations adopted across the country;
  • An analysis of their diffusion and actual adoption by farmers;
  • An assessment of the public policies that support their development.

The official launch took place on May 15, 2025 in Abidjan, during a workshop held at the Silver Moon hotel. The event brought together researchers, public decision-makers, agricultural stakeholders and technical partners. It aimed to present the project, mobilize stakeholders and encourage their active engagement.

In her opening remarks, Ms. Kouadio Sylvie Zoh, representing the Director General of Planning, Statistics and Projects at MEMINADER, welcomed the project’s participatory approach and emphasized the importance of involving local actors for the effective orientation of public and private investments. She noted that this initiative paves the way for a more resilient, inclusive and sustainable Ivorian agriculture, grounded in science, innovation and consultation.

Professor Ahoure Alban, Director of CAPEC, closed the workshop by thanking participants for their commitment. He recalled that the project embodies a collective approach—rooted in local realities while inspired by international best practices—and stressed the decisive role of research in informing public policies and improving the well-being of rural populations.

news30.title: Marketing Methods and Techniques: BNETD Executives at CAPEC School
news30.excerpt: Specialized training in marketing methods and techniques for BNETD executives.
news30.mot:
Marketing Methods and Techniques: BNETD Executives at CAPEC School
  1. In order to improve the quality of its services in the field of Marketing, the National Bureau of Technical Studies and Development (BNETD), in collaboration with CAPEC, offered a capacity-building opportunity to executives from its Marketing and Communication Unit. The theme selected for this five-day training was: "Developing a marketing study/survey". The opening ceremony took place on Monday, September 21, 2020, at BNETD, in the presence of Prof. Kamgnia Bernadette, Deputy Director of CAPEC, and Mr. Romuald Kodjo, BNETD Training Officer. Both praised the opportunity and encouraged participants to be committed and diligent.
  2. The overall objective of the training was to provide participants with appropriate methods and techniques for conducting a marketing study/survey. More specifically, the workshop focused on defining the fundamental concepts of marketing research, including marketing information needs, core questions related to management, planning and product development, as well as recent developments in market research.
  3. According to Mr. KOUAKOU Koffi Valerie, Associate Trainer at CAPEC, the methodology for this training was primarily based on an andragogical approach that promotes exchanges between trainers and learners. It combined theoretical presentations, illustrative examples and case studies. In total, seven (07) modules were delivered, namely: Discover the Marketing approach; Carry out a marketing diagnosis; Understand the methodology of market research; Develop and implement the questionnaire; and Turn study results into Marketing tools.
  4. Mayane Yapo, Communication and Visibility Officer, CAPEC

  5. Location: BNETD, Abidjan
  6. Participants: 3 participants

A scientific methodology and writing workshop was held in Abidjan from April 1 to 5
  1. A scientific methodology and writing workshop organized by the Council for the Development of Social Science Research in Africa (CODESRIA), in collaboration with the Economic Policy Analysis Unit of CIRES (CAPEC), was held in Abidjan from April 1 to 5, 2019.

  2. This meeting, organized for newly selected MRI members, aimed to help them improve their proposals, prepare them for research and scientific writing, and foster a friendly atmosphere and network dynamics among group members.

  3. Participants from several African countries attended presentations delivered by resource persons during a series of highly participatory and interactive sessions.

  4. As a reminder, CODESRIA was created in 1973. Its headquarters are located in Dakar, Senegal. Its main mandate is to promote social science research in all regions of Africa.

  5. The awardees also thanked CAPEC for the opportunity provided. They praised the relevance of the themes and congratulated the trainers and organizers on the smooth running of the workshop, notably regarding the adequacy of the logistical and pedagogical resources deployed by CAPEC.

  6. They also noted, through their spokesperson, that the positive results achieved during this capacity-building session will contribute to improving the performance of their respective services, for better monitoring of industrial development actions toward Côte d'Ivoire’s emergence by 2020, in line with the expectations of the 2016–2020 National Development Plan (PND).

  7. It should be noted that the Directorate General for Industrial Activity (DGAI) is led by Mr. Komenan Mougo, who is also President of CAPEC’s Steering Committee.

  8. Mayane Yapo, Communication and Visibility Officer, CAPEC

news24.title: KAIZEN Project in Côte d'Ivoire
news24.excerpt: Launch and implementation of the KAIZEN project for continuous productivity improvement in Côte d'Ivoire.
news24.mot:
KAIZEN Project in Côte d’Ivoire
  1. Côte d’Ivoire benefits from technical support from the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) as part of the implementation of the Small and Medium Enterprise Promotion Project, also known as the KAIZEN Project. This project will run from July 2025 to August 2028 and aims to strengthen quality, productivity and competitiveness along agricultural and agri-food value chains.
  2. KAIZEN, a Japanese term meaning “continuous improvement,” is a management philosophy that—through practical tools such as the 5S method—helps reduce waste, improve organization and increase company performance.
  3. As part of the project, training for Ivorian consultants on the 5S/KAIZEN approach is being held from September 15 to 26, 2025 in Abidjan and includes theoretical sessions and a practical in-company phase. CAPEC, as a partner structure, will host a consultant tasked with applying the KAIZEN method within CIRES from September 23 to 25, 2025.
  4. This project is a strategic lever to spread the culture of continuous improvement, develop local skills and enhance the competitiveness of Ivorian companies.

news23.title: Three New Doctors in Economics Trained at CAPEC
news23.excerpt: Three new Doctors in Economics trained within the Economic Policy Analysis Unit of CIRES.
news23.mot:
Three new Doctors in Economics trained within CAPEC
  1. The Economic Policy Analysis Unit of CIRES (CAPEC) is proud to honor three of its PhD candidates who have successfully defended their doctoral dissertations in Economics—an important milestone in their academic and professional journeys.
    YEO Kolotioloma Innocent Hamed
  1. He joined CAPEC in November 2017 under the GEMMES project (GEneral Monetary and Multisectoral Macrodynamics for the Ecological Shift) – Côte d’Ivoire, an initiative stemming from a strategic memorandum signed between the Ministry of Planning and Development and the French Development Agency (AFD). Within this project, he contributed as a PhD candidate and research assistant to the development of a structural macroeconomic demand model to inform public policies.
  2. Supervised by Professor ESSO Loesse Jacques (Chief of Staff to the Minister of Trade and Industry and former Deputy Director of CAPEC), he defended on July 23, 2025 at Alassane Ouattara University in Bouaké his dissertation entitled ‘Essays on the informal economy’. His work analyzes the effect of informality on permanent employment and the strategies for formalization.
  3. He reaches the following conclusions:
    • (i) informality reduces permanent employment through firms’ turnover;
    • (ii) public consumption is a budgetary lever to limit the informal economy;
    • (iii) innovation can play an important role in reducing the size of the informal economy.
    KESSE Tano Koutoua Devez
  1. He joined CAPEC in November 2017 as a research assistant and PhD candidate during the implementation of the GEMMES project – Côte d’Ivoire. He distinguished himself through a key contribution to building a macro-structural model applied to the Ivorian economy, in collaboration with AFD.
  2. He successfully defended his PhD dissertation at Alassane Ouattara University in Bouaké on the analysis of the effects of commodity price shocks on Ivorian public finances and mitigation strategies to reduce their impact.
  3. His work was conducted under the scientific supervision of Professor ESSO Loesse Jacques, former Deputy Director of CAPEC and current Chief of Staff to the Minister of Trade and Industry.
  4. His research interests—macroeconomic modeling, international macroeconomics and applied econometrics—reflect a strong desire to put economic science at the service of public action, particularly in a context marked by vulnerability to exogenous shocks.

📍 EPA Forum – In partnership with ACED

The EPA Forum, organized in partnership with ACED, was held in Abidjan on November 6 and 7, 2024. This major event brought together key development actors from various backgrounds to collectively reflect on pathways toward inclusive development in Francophone Africa.

The first day began with an informal session designed to create a climate of trust conducive to open and constructive exchanges. This introduction was followed by a series of in-depth discussions on national ecosystems for the production and use of evidence in countries across the region.

A highlight of the day was the official launch of the Regional Community of Practice—an initiative bringing together several African countries to share experiences, know-how and good practices in evidence-informed public policies.

The day concluded with a “solutions marketplace,” a dynamic exchange space where innovative initiatives were presented, notably in the fight against misinformation—an important issue for governance and citizen participation.

The second day focused on the central role of evidence in achieving sustainable and equitable development. Participants discussed several structuring themes, such as financing African research, valuing local knowledge, and challenges linked to political transitions on the continent.

Concrete recommendations were formulated at the end of the discussions to improve financing and the structuring of evidence ecosystems in Africa—an essential condition for effectively guiding public policies and strengthening the capacities of local actors.

news8.mot:
2023 – Year of Youth – CAPEC: a tool to guide public policies for young people’s socio-professional integration
  1. CAPEC conducted a research project on “Impact study of the socio-economic integration of vulnerable youth in Côte d’Ivoire”, funded by the Partnership for Economic Policy (PEP) and Canada’s International Development Research Centre (IDRC). The study used the post-conflict context of Côte d'Ivoire to assess the impact of citizenship training on the social inclusion of vulnerable youth. Using a randomized controlled trial (RCT), the intervention shows a positive impact on reducing crime, drug use, alcohol consumption and violent traits, on the one hand, and significant positive effects on altruism, positive reciprocity, risk preference and life satisfaction, on the other. However, the program has a positive and significant effect on impatience, life dissatisfaction and impulsivity among women, indicating a certain gender bias. The conclusions of this evaluation guided the Ivorian government’s decision to scale up civic service centers during the Council of Ministers on July 7, 2021.
  2. CAPEC received funding from Canada’s IDRC and from PEP to implement a research project analyzing public policies related to COVID-19 for vulnerable people and businesses in four (4) African countries: Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire and Senegal. This project included an experimental study component on “evaluating mitigation measures for the effects of COVID-19 on vulnerable youth”. The objective was to provide an intervention (public policy) to these youth in the form of social protection, implemented through three modules (mitigation package): a cash transfer, an information campaign on COVID-19, and entrepreneurship education, within an RCT framework. The mitigation package had a significant impact on beliefs and concerns about COVID-19. The program also had a positive and significant effect on the propensity to comply with social distancing. Estimation results show that the program has the potential to instill an entrepreneurial culture among vulnerable youth; indeed, it increases the propensity for entrepreneurship by nearly 30%.

int1.title: "Our research will help establish a link between youth violence and economic opportunities"
int1.speaker: Prof Kimou Assi José Carlos, Senior Researcher at CAPEC, Head of Research and Monitoring-Evaluation
int1.content:
CAPEC recently launched a third collaborative project funded by IDRC, focused on the theme: "Analysis of the effect of youth employability on urban violence in the post-conflict period in Côte d'Ivoire." Why this theme?

Côte d'Ivoire experienced a decade of instability that was a source of intense violence. We note that at the socio-economic environment level, violence is an element that can disrupt a country's development trajectory. Because, in a context of violence, there can be less investment, less wealth creation, loss of human life, deterioration of human capital built through training and education, erosion of social capital (people trust each other less, suspicion sets in between communities), etc.

All these elements combined can disrupt the wealth creation trajectory and slow economic growth. In the context of Côte d'Ivoire, we realize that it is this decade of instability that generated violence throughout the country in terms of inter-group conflicts. In communities, in everyday life, we witness the emergence of new forms of violence among young people commonly called children in conflict with the law or "microbes" and the growing number of assaults perpetrated in different sectors and different regions of the country. Such a concern cannot be overlooked in a research agenda aimed at policy formation.

What is the state of precariousness of young people in Côte d'Ivoire? And why are you particularly interested in this segment of the population?

Young people are indeed the most capable of producing violence if they are not occupied legally and legitimately in the labor market. However, in the case of Côte d'Ivoire, during the entire period of instability, young people were the most negatively impacted by the decline in economic activity levels or poverty levels. Data from the National Institute of Statistics (INS) from a standard of living survey (ENV) conducted in 2018 showed that out of 10 poor people in Côte d'Ivoire, 7 are young people under 25 who have no legal and legitimate occupation. It is therefore likely that these young people resort to violence as an alternative source of survival. We therefore want to know the link that can be established between these realities.

The study therefore focuses more on young people because they constitute the highest proportion (+60%) of the population in developing countries and particularly in Côte d'Ivoire. This youth, which constitutes the active workforce, when not involved in legal or legitimate activities, occupies itself otherwise by most often resorting to violence. This is especially true since the living conditions of young people aged 15 to 35 have sufficiently deteriorated.

Indeed, youth unemployment was estimated at +12% according to the 2012 employment survey, compared to the national average of 9%. The 2016 employment situation survey (ENSESI, 2016), although indicating a relatively low unemployment rate (2.8%), confirms this trend with a higher unemployment rate among young people aged 14-24 (3.9%) and in the 25-35 age group (3.5%).

Where do you classify "children in conflict with the law" who have no income-generating activities?

Violence can be perpetrated individually or in groups. Children in conflict with the law fall into this second category of young people who band together to perpetrate acts of violence. This behavior is fundamentally motivated by the quest for means of subsistence given that these children are destitute and very vulnerable.

Indeed, studies have been conducted in Bouaké that reveal that the perpetrators of violence in the transport sector are public transport drivers or two-wheeled vehicle operators. It is the same situation in Abidjan where victims reported being assaulted in the transport sector.

We therefore want to conduct investigations not only to know the impact of this phenomenon in the transport sector, but also to understand the importance of this sector in the sources of violence. We start from the following concern: what links exist between employability and violence? More specifically, we will try to provide elements of answers to the following questions:

- Can violence be reduced or curbed by offering employment opportunities to vulnerable youth such as "children in conflict with the law"?

- Despite the reforms that have taken place in the public transport sector, does the State have an interest in prohibiting this type of activity?

- Do training programs allow young people released from prison to integrate, abandon violence, or reoffend?

How do you define violence in simpler terms?

There is no clear-cut definition of violence because this concept embraces several fields. However, we refer to the WHO definition accepted within the scientific community. It presents violence as the intentional use of physical force, threats against a group or community that can result in trauma (emotional, psychological, physical, death, etc.).

Which target is most impacted?

The angle we have chosen to address in this study is interested in the supply of violence (those who commit violence) and not the demand for violence (the victims). The question may suggest victims. However, we are not really interested in victims who encompass everyone insofar as we consider that violence produces negative externalities for all. This research project is rather interested in the production, the supply of violence. Who is at the origin of violence? In my introductory remarks, I presented violence through the prism of the exercise of physical force. This involves those who have the physical capacity to produce this physical force, and these are young people with certain physical dispositions in terms of activities.

Note also that this research project excludes political violence and/or politically justified violence (war, terrorism, riots, etc.).

How do you measure violence?

From an economic point of view, violence can be measured in several ways. One of the first possibilities concerns police data that records all acts of violence and groups together a set of indicators enshrined in judicial procedures (homicides, armed robberies, assaults, etc.). The police can therefore collect this information and give an idea of the level of violence prevailing in a community. However, it should be noted that for research purposes, this information suffers from a number of limitations.

Firstly, this data is only collected when the victim files a complaint or when the police have been alerted. This means that this information may be underestimated and may not reflect the reality of the phenomenon. Furthermore, this data is said to be aggregated data and does not allow us to know the profile of the perpetrators of such acts.

Another approach is to be able to conduct victimization surveys which, conducted under very good conditions, lead individuals to reveal their experiences of violence. This allows us to capture the level of magnitude of the phenomenon. This is a method widely used in the literature. In our case, we are only interested in the producers of violence and not the victims. We therefore do not go in this direction.

We can also rely on self-reported data by the individual who states that they themselves participated or did not participate in violence activities in terms of attitude, belief about violence. But there too, this data can produce "white noise," that is to say that the individual may briefly tell you what you want to hear and not reveal the true information.

To correct this state of affairs, we use in addition to other methods, vignettes which are a situational scenario allowing us to capture the cognitive and psychological evaluation of the agent's behavior. We therefore advocate a behavioral approach in measuring violence that allows us to get as close as possible to these behaviors.

Which sectors are most affected by violence in Côte d'Ivoire?

In the aftermath of the return to normalcy after the decade of crisis, we noticed a resurgence of certain forms of violence in particular sectors, notably in the transport sector. Here, young people in gangs commonly called "coxers" assault passersby to impose and control a set of resources. There is also the motorcycle taxi sector in certain regions of the country, where young people also exercise violence.

By focusing on the transport sector in general, our study will seek to know if it is a sector of propagation or resilience that helps counter the issue of violence since young people who perpetrate violence can take refuge there to have a legitimate occupation and restore themselves socially.

The transport sector seems to be the most impacted?

Not necessarily, but it is one of the sectors where we have statistics that describe the magnitude of the phenomenon a bit more. Otherwise, in everyday life, youth violence manifests everywhere.

The impact of violence seems to be only negative. Can there be a positive impact and what can be the cost of violence for the State?

If we start from the hypothesis that violence is a source of negative externality (a set of elements not controlled by the market), certainly there can be beneficial elements that can be a war economy, an underground economy (money laundering), but I am not sure that a legitimate State can prioritize this aspect of things. On the other hand, a State would want to have peaceful socio-economic conditions that encourage private initiative, where agents' properties are protected so as to create prosperity. This represents an enormous cost for the State and the opposite could mean that the State is failing and this would discourage investments. The State will therefore not have fiscal resources to finance all social programs of education, health, etc. Ultimately, the costs are enormous. Work has estimated these costs in terms of loss of growth points, loss of human life (human capital).

Are you aware of measures taken by the Government to curb or prevent violence among young people?

After 2012, the Ivorian Government worked to accelerate economic growth so as to create more wealth and opportunities and contribute to post-conflict stability, with an important focus on youth employability. There have been several initiatives but what we want to look at in our research project are those in favor of young people with a certain level of vulnerability, particularly "children in conflict with the law." The State has established the Civic Service for Employment and Development (SCAED) which aims to identify these young people evolving in gangs, on the margins of the proper functioning of society, to reintegrate them via civic service by giving them vocational training and helping them to settle so that they can take care of themselves and become model citizens contributing to wealth creation.

We want to know if this program really works? Does it really contribute to reducing violence? If so, what are the positive aspects and if it doesn't work, what are the aspects to correct? We will therefore study the impact of this program.

There is another initiative in favor of minors (-18 years) in prisons. The State, through the support of certain NGOs, has undertaken to re-educate minors placed under provisional custody orders, through dedicated observation centers. We were able to visit this type of program at the Abidjan House of Arrest and Correction (MACA) and the Bouaké House of Arrest and Correction to see how it works. It is about identifying a cohort of young people and following them over two or three passages to understand the functioning in terms of behavioral change, possibility of integration.

There have been other government measures in the two-wheeled transport sector (motorcyclists or tricycles). Here, we want to know if prohibiting these young people from practicing this type of profession is effective. Or if it is not better to organize them, structure them better to give them the chance to have a decent standard of living. Ultimately, we will seek to know if this sector is not a place of resilience and prevention of youth violence.

What objectives underlie the problem on which the research project focuses?

The main objective of our work is to analyze the link between the economic opportunity represented here by youth employability and youth violence. If we manage to analyze a few specific objectives such as the impact of employment access programs on violence in the public transport sector; the impact of youth reintegration programs in prisons; if we manage to produce evidence, factual and convincing data, we should be able to achieve our ultimate objective which is to provide economic policy recommendations to inform decision-making.

What relationship can exist between violence and economic opportunities?

It should be noted that this study is conducted by a multidisciplinary team composed notably of economists and sociologists. From an economic point of view, if you take an individual in full possession of their faculties, they have a choice between two alternatives: either they occupy themselves legally, or they occupy themselves illegally. In both cases, the individual takes into account a set of factors that allow them to engage based on the highest gain. Our concern is as follows: if economic opportunities are offered to young people, would this allow them to exercise a legal or legitimate occupation and leave the circle of violence? Through this research project, we therefore want to establish a link between youth violence and economic opportunities.

What are the structures involved in this project?

This collaborative research project funded by IDRC brings together a cohort of five (05) research centers: The Research Institute (IREM) of Benin, the Applied Analysis Research Group of Burkina (GRAAB), the Kenyan Center for Research and Innovation, South Africa is also represented as well as the Economic Policy Analysis Cell of Cires (CAPEC) for Côte d'Ivoire.

What will be your work agenda?

The different activities that fall within the framework of this research project lasting approximately two and a half years are linked to our methodology. We adopt an experimental approach that will include data collection. We will have a launch ceremony which will be followed by a stakeholder meeting to promote ownership by the parties involved. A capacity building component is also included for young researchers preparing their theses on these issues. Articles from the research work will also be presented during forums, conferences and other major scientific meetings. It will mainly be about producing from all this work a good economic policy document that will serve as decision support.

Interview conducted by Mayane YAPO, Communication and Visibility Officer at CAPEC

int2.title: "Côte d'Ivoire has not regressed but its progress has been less significant"
int2.speaker: Dr. Germain Kramo, Researcher at CAPEC
int2.content:
CÔTE D'IVOIRE'S RANKING IN THE LATEST DOING BUSINESS 2020 REPORT

1. What do you think of the performance achieved by Côte d'Ivoire in the Doing Business 2020 report?

Overall, Côte d'Ivoire has progressed in the ranking of the 2020 edition of Doing Business. It gained 12 places, moving from 122nd place in 2018 to 110th place in 2019. Côte d'Ivoire's score increased from 58 to 60.7.

According to the report, the main reforms implemented by Côte d'Ivoire in 2019 focus on:

- Facilitating tax payment through online payments

- Facilitating contract enforcement by publishing reports on the results of commercial courts and case developments.

2. Côte d'Ivoire has dropped out of the top 10 most reforming countries in the world. Is this an underperformance?

Côte d'Ivoire has not regressed but its progress has been less significant than that of other countries that entered the top 10. The score increased by 2.7 points between 2018 and 2019. Whereas the score had increased by 4.29 points between 2017 and 2018.

On the other hand, if we consider the forecasts of the NDP 2016-2020, we could say that Côte d'Ivoire has achieved poor performance because it projected to be in the top 50 of the Doing Business ranking in 2019 with a score of 72 while it is now ranked 110th with a score of 60.7.

3. What are the explanatory factors for this underperformance by Côte d'Ivoire?

Several factors could explain this result:

- First, there is fatigue. The country has been engaged in a process of improving the business environment since 2011. As such, it has carried out several reforms. So 8 years after the start of this marathon to improve the business environment, the country is somewhat exhausted;

- Second, there is the impact of the political cycle. The country will engage in an electoral cycle in 2020. Consequently, making reforms may not be the priority of leaders at the moment. According to the political cycle theory, as elections approach, social issues become the priority of leaders. This is once again verified with the development and implementation of the government's social program called "PS Gouv";

- Third, the strong progress of other countries should also be noted. This is the case of Togo which entered the top 10.

4. What are the areas in which Côte d'Ivoire should make efforts to improve its performance?

Côte d'Ivoire's score is 60.7 in the 2020 edition of Doing Business. There are areas where the score is well below the country's overall score. These areas where Côte d'Ivoire performs poorly pull the overall score down. There are at least seven (7) areas in which Côte d'Ivoire must make significant efforts. These are:

- the number of procedures to obtain a building permit: a score of 32 out of 100. Well below the overall score of 60.7;

- the number of procedures to access electricity: a score of 16.67 out of 100;

- the protection of minority shareholders: a score of 42 out of 100;

- the protection of minority shareholders: Extent of ownership and control: a score of 28.57 out of 100;

- property registration: quality of administration in charge of land property registration: a score of 33.33 out of 100;

- resolving insolvency: a score of 47.93 out of 100;

- resolving insolvency: recovery rate: a score of 39.62 out of 100.

Reforms in these areas will improve the country's score and achieve the objective set in the NDP 2016-2020 which is to be in the top 50 of the doing business ranking in 2020 with a score of 72 points.

5- Isn't it too late to undertake these reforms? 2020 is in two (2) months

Improving the business environment is a perpetual quest. So it is never too late to make reforms. Countries are in competition. Each country seeks to be as attractive as possible. In addition, the next report, that of 2021, will be produced in about a year. So it is not too late to undertake these reforms.

6- Can you recall what "Doing Business" is. What are the objectives assigned to it? How many countries are concerned?

The Doing Business project is an initiative of the World Bank Group, which measures business regulation and its effective application. At the launch of the project in 2002, the project covered 183 countries. In the 2020 edition, 190 economies are ranked.

The objective is to provide an objective basis for understanding and improving the regulatory business environment around the world by collecting and analyzing detailed quantitative data to compare regulatory frameworks applicable to businesses worldwide over time.

int3.title: "One does not become a Full Professor through personal work alone."
int3.speaker: Prof Mama Ouattara, Director of Cires
int3.content:
Prof. Mama Ouattara: "One does not become a Full Professor through personal work alone".

What does this tenure represent for you?

It is the crowning achievement of an academic career and therefore of all the efforts made to enrich it. Every academic should have the objective of finishing their career at the rank of Full Professor, because in doing so, they prove the consistency between their career choice and their abilities. I therefore naturally feel pride in belonging to this rank, especially since the evaluation is done by teachers from several countries. It is a real moral and intellectual satisfaction for me to know that there is compatibility between my choice and my abilities. Beyond that, it must be emphasized that this denotes the dynamism of Research in Côte d'Ivoire, despite the problem of lack of research funding which constitutes a brake on its development.

Why wait so long (since you have been tenured since 1991), to access the rank of Full Professor?

You know, it's not as easy as one might imagine. First, you must be able to become aware of the obstacles that one can encounter in the quest for this tenure and then display the will to overcome them by giving yourself the means. Then, there is the fact that when you choose a research subject, it is like a marriage you have just entered into. You have to maintain it and devote yourself to it entirely. However, we often let ourselves go to the desire to want to enjoy time because the urgency of passing this milestone does not systematically appear. Yet, the candidate for tenure must do more than the tenured Associate Professor and show their ability to deal with different subjects in Economics. Note that if tenure is obtained much more through individual work, full professorship can only be obtained through collective work. The results depending on those you supervise (since you are required to train doctoral students) and your own supervisors. At this level, I would like to express all my gratitude to my supervisors, notably, Professor Aké G. M. N'GBO who helped me a lot.

You were at your second attempt after an unfortunate first experience in 2005.

Indeed, I tried in 2005 and it didn't work out. I didn't give up. I tried to understand what didn't work and I got to work. So I take this opportunity to tell young people that they must understand that when a candidate fails, it is not because their supervisors are against them, but because they do not meet one of the required conditions. Rather than looking for arguments to exonerate themselves, the candidate would benefit from being humble and persevering.

int4.title: "Results-Based Management can help Southern countries achieve their development objectives"
int4.speaker: Jean AMANTCHI GOGOUA, Senior Economist World Bank
int4.content:
Could you say, in a few words, what RBM is and situate it in its context?

Increasingly, technical and financial partners of Southern country governments pay attention to the use of resources allocated to them. Southern countries are also called upon to implement development strategies for which populations actually expect results. There is, moreover, a global movement towards transparency and increased accountability in the management of public affairs. Monitoring and evaluation mechanisms are also gaining importance. In this context, Results-Based Management presents itself as an approach, an instrumental procedure that can help Southern countries achieve their development objectives.

It is a set of tools that must be implemented to address the challenges related to development effectiveness. Increasingly, you will hear about development effectiveness that goes beyond aid effectiveness. These issues are gaining momentum and one of the management approaches to address them is RBM. Countries will be more rigorous in developing their sectoral strategies or their national development strategies. They will be more rigorous and relevant in the effective implementation of these strategies, in their monitoring and evaluation and in the lessons they can draw from them. All of this therefore calls for governments to make the choice to focus their daily and strategic actions (long-term) on the effective delivery of results. Hence, RBM.

To summarize, RBM is a public management approach that directs resources towards achieving results. This calls for a certain number of adjustments on the part of public managers and decision-makers. Issues of transparency, accountability, obligation of results gain momentum when moving towards an RBM approach.

What are the principles of Results-Based Management?

The first principle of RBM is that of participation: governments must agree with the citizens for whom they undertake activities and on the results to be achieved. Donors have also committed, within the framework of the Paris Declaration on Aid Effectiveness, in 2005, to support our governments for the implementation of RBM.

The second important principle is that of the question of national leadership on development results: nothing will be imposed henceforth. Donors are ready to align themselves with the strategic choices for the development of our countries. This is about the ownership of development challenges by aid recipient countries.

After the focus on results, it is the mechanism for structuring programs and projects focused on these results. It is about focusing on the entire implementation process of these programs and projects to which we have committed ourselves with the beneficiary populations. These populations are in reality, within the framework of the RBM approach, seen as "clients" of the governors.

There is also the principle that relates to result measurement mechanisms: a set of performance indicators and targets that must be defined, validated and allowing the monitoring of the implementation of projects and programs. Within the framework of RBM, evaluation takes on importance. It would be inconceivable that from now on we have public institutions without reinforced, relevant departments or services in charge of evaluating programs and projects. How could we structure future projects and programs if we have not learned lessons from what was done previously? This would make no sense!

Within the framework of RBM, the notions of accountability, delegation take on importance. Prior control is relaxed to strengthen posterior control. Processes certainly, but adjusted to allow achieving development results. There is a set of institutional mutations and management approaches (what the Americans call "New public Management"), in which the RBM approach fits. Our countries (especially Côte d'Ivoire), should move in this framework. The development challenges in this country are such that there is a need to put on the table and adopt the Results-Based Management approach. This is not empty rhetoric. It is in everyday behaviors that we see the mutation. I want to emphasize, this change does not happen in one day. RBM is an approach that includes a learning process. We always learn lessons from the past to improve. It is important that our governments commit to it.

A distinction was noted during the training workshop between SMART and CREAM performance indicators. Would you like to come back to these indicators.

We have always heard in the speeches of technical and financial partners who support our governments, SMART indicators. In reality, when we structure our programs and projects, there are performance indicators and targets that cover each year of the project or program. The CREAM+ (Clear-Relevant-Economic-Adequate-Monitorible) criteria are applied to the specification and validation of performance indicators. The "+" explains that if you have two or three indicators in addition to an initially adopted indicator, the additional indicator that you will choose must give additional information.

SMART criteria are criteria for choosing and validating targets. The target must be specific to the indicator, it must be measurable, achievable and realistic. If you have a target that does not take into account the constraints you have, that it is in reality utopian and therefore unattainable, this means that the results to which you commit are not relevant. The target must be time-bound, otherwise you are flying blind! These are subtleties that are important in results-based project budgeting. When you have your indicator and your target, you are able to do costing, budgeting of your project for each year.

In the impact chain, do you think that the absence or insufficiency of an element could lead to the failure of results?

First, it should be noted that the impact chain is the results chain. These are levels that allow us to monitor and know that the projects as they have been structured make sense, that they contribute to development objectives, either sectoral or national. As a reminder, the impact chain, at the first level, consists of the means that must be mobilized (physical and financial resources) to roll out activities to obtain outputs. The use of outputs allows having effects that translate, in time, into impact. Without means, you cannot carry out your activities and if you do not have activities, you cannot deliver your products and services. These products and services, if they are not delivered, produce no effect and without effect, you have, ultimately, no impact. The impact chain is the RBM analysis cycle. When embarking on project preparation, it is important to know its common thread which is the impact chain.

You mentioned, during your presentation, a series of questions that should be asked before undertaking an activity. Could you come back to this?

People want to do everything because they want to be seen everywhere. Are they undertaking activities that contribute to achieving development objectives and results? Do these activities respond to the challenges that their sector or the country, as a whole, faces? Here for example are some questions that each of us and especially public managers should ask themselves. The first level of question that we should actually ask ourselves is: "Are we doing the right things?" The second level, "Are we doing things right?" These are the types of questions that RBM poses.

Managing for and not by results, what does that mean?

When structuring one's strategic plan, one's priority projects or programs, there are a number of results that should be achieved. Take for example development results. You should for example, build classrooms to school young girls, in the north of Côte d'Ivoire. When you have these classrooms, you actually need these young girls to come register and regularly attend classes. If while you have classrooms, you have no students, it is said that you have managed for results. You were not really in an approach oriented on development results. You certainly undertook things but which were not correct. We had in Côte d'Ivoire, village pumps that were rehabilitated without the villagers using them. These are actions that did not respond to development challenges.

The advantages of strategic planning?

No public or private decision-maker and even a household can fly blind. Strategic planning consists of giving oneself fundamentals, pillars, a framework of orientation for the future. It is necessary to plan taking into account: environmental challenges, one's internal organization, Human Resources capacities, population needs. When one plans, one is able to face resource constraints insofar as one has a priority of programs and projects that can be adjusted over time. Planning therefore allows guiding public action. It is not even necessary to make a plea for results-based strategic planning. It goes without saying. When strategic planning is done, it is then necessary to conduct results-based operational planning that includes for each year, an annual work plan and budgeting. It is in this type of approach that Ivorian and African administrations, in general, must commit more than ever! The challenges and social needs are enormous, we cannot therefore continue to fly blind.

deb1.title: "Mr. Director, what could be the short or medium-term impacts of the confinement measure following the health situation related to COVID-19?"
deb1.participants: Prof AHOURE Alban. Director of Capec
deb1.content:
The question asked concerns not the impact of the disease itself but the impact of an important consequence which is confinement or the set of prevention and protection measures taken by the Ivorian Government, like governments of other countries. These barrier measures concern the closure of outdoor restaurants, bars, restaurants, the isolation of "Greater Abidjan," provisions for limiting the number of people during gatherings, limiting the number of seats in public transport vehicles, etc.

In terms of impact, what we are trying to do at CAPEC with other institutions is to be able to make assessments.

At the microeconomic level, there are job and household income losses, violence against women, women's workload at home due to the confinement of children, increased food expenditures while incomes are falling, etc. There were surveys conducted by the National Institute of Statistics (INS) with the support of UNDP and the World Bank over the period from April 11 to 18, 2020, just one month after the measures were taken. In total, as of mid-April 2020 (survey conducted from April 11 to 18, 2020) an actual job loss of 22,962 or 4.03% of modern jobs (22,224 jobs or 3.9% for SMEs) compared to 738 for large companies or 0.13%) relative to modern jobs of companies registered in the INS financial database (2017). The most affected sectors in terms of employment are: the transport and storage sector: decrease of 53.5%; the accommodation and food service sector: decrease of 37.2%, and the agri-food sector a decrease of 29.7%.

Regarding industrial production units (IPU), compared to March 2019, 1,656,595 IPUs or 88.1% experienced a decrease in their turnover from the onset of the crisis (March 2020). Overall, more than 94% of IPU heads estimate that the health crisis affects their activities. Abidjan is the most affected with a proportion of 98.7% of these IPUs.

More than half of households (71.7%) suffered a decrease in income. The average annual income of household heads goes from 722,801.8 FCFA to 405,770.4 FCFA, representing an average decrease of 43.9%. More than 31.5% of household heads feel a decrease in income varying between 45% and 65%. 57.7% of households suffered an increase in their food expenditures, 47% in their communication expenditures and 25.6% in their non-food expenditures (hydroalcoholic gel, mask, bucket, etc.). It is noted that 45.2% go from a status of non-poor to poor, or 1,620,777 additional households. The poverty situation of 16.51% of households has worsened due to the fact that they were below the poverty line before the health crisis and their income has further decreased (on average by 30%). This situation makes them even more vulnerable.

At the macroeconomic level, CAPEC conducted a study that showed that the health response and prevention plan including distancing measures and the isolation of Greater Abidjan resulted in losses of working time, and a decrease in foreign direct investment should be expected because the health crisis is global and affects almost all countries at once. According to a UNCTAD report published on March 27, 2020, the outbreak and expansion of the Covid-19 pandemic will result in a dramatic decrease in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) flows. Revisions of investment plans by the largest multinational firms indicate that the decrease in FDI could be -30% to -40% in 2020-2021. On average, the 5,000 largest multinational companies in the world have revised downward by about 30% their investment forecasts for 2020 and this decrease could intensify.

These elements combined showed through the analyses carried out for the Ministry of Economy and Finance, that there is a decrease in economic growth of 3.6 percentage points compared to the forecast of 7.2% for 2020, i.e., an economic growth rate of 3.6%, if the crisis is controlled by the end of June 2020.

Another more pessimistic scenario predicts a decrease of 5.7 percentage points compared to the initial forecast for 2020, i.e., a growth rate of 1.5% if the government takes no measures. A catastrophic scenario gives growth close to 0 or even negative if the crisis lasts longer and nothing is done.

The most affected sectors remain those of hospitality, catering, transport, industry but also finance. This last sector will be impacted because companies or households that have borrowed will no longer be able to repay loans on time. At the State level, tax revenues are declining because companies can no longer pay taxes.

These ex-ante forecasts of the macroeconomic impact of the pandemic, carried out in March 2020, will have to be re-evaluated in light of the measures taken by the Government through the social, economic and humanitarian response plan of 1,700 billion FCFA, announced by the Prime Minister on March 30, 2020 and which is being implemented. This plan consists of transfers to the most vulnerable households, to those who have lost their jobs especially in the formal sector, support to formal and informal businesses and to certain strategic production sectors at the agricultural level, etc. All these measures taken by the Ivorian Government should help mitigate, reduce the estimated impacts or anticipated impacts of the pandemic on households, businesses and even on public finances. CAPEC is pleased to have contributed alongside the relevant services of the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF) and all stakeholders to the identification of these response measures.

An ex-post evaluation, which takes into account the effects of the pandemic on supply and demand, as well as the measures taken, now appears necessary to better understand the net effect of Covid-19 on the Ivorian economy, while considering the uncertainty regarding the end of the health crisis both nationally and globally. The approach to evaluating the impacts (microeconomic and macroeconomic) of the health crisis and the measures taken, must thus be done dynamically (updating assumptions/measures, in simulations and conducting surveys again), to have results closer to reality as the crisis and the socio-economic environment evolve.

deb2.title: "What lessons can Africans draw from the franc zone?"
deb2.participants: Dr. Fatou Sow (CAPEC), Dr. Ouattara Ibrahim (CNRA), Mrs. Bamba Aminata (Ministry of Agriculture)
deb2.content:
"The monetary question is sometimes a question of sovereignty, independence and national dignity..."

We observe that what economists had said about the optimal monetary zone is being verified today. European countries do not meet the conditions to form an optimal monetary zone. This is what emerges from this eurozone crisis.

What lessons for us Africans, members of the Euro zone - because the franc zone is a misnomer, it no longer exists! Is Côte d'Ivoire, Gabon qualified to be in the same monetary zone as Germany? The essential question is as follows: an African currency for what purpose? It is necessary to know what type of currency it is (regional or national). Confusion must be avoided. At the national level, we need a currency to develop, to do things ourselves. Even if we must have problems with a currency that we create, we will create it anyway until we know how to manage a currency. WAEMU countries perhaps had nothing to exchange when the CFA was created in the 1960s. Today, we are attached to it. There is no clear-cut position, the question must be treated case by case.

I nevertheless join Prof. ONDO OSSA in saying that the monetary question is sometimes a question of sovereignty, independence and national dignity even if this sovereignty is now compromised and we are moving towards collective sovereignty. We should not completely reject the idea of trying to create an African or West African currency. The essential thing is sequencing: going step by step, giving ourselves the means to go there progressively. At the end of this whole process, there is the problem of national, regional or political sovereignty.
